I'm going to keep this short because you probably have a standup in an hour and a 1:1 you're not quite ready for after that.

subject_variants.subject: Nobody told you it was a different job
The thing under the thing you're actually struggling with
Why the management books aren't helping

welcome_seq.preview: It's not that you're bad at this. It's that you're doing a job nobody explained.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

You got promoted because you were the best engineer in the room.

Then someone changed the job description without telling you, handed you a 90-minute e-learning module about SMART goals, and called it preparation.

The 1:1s feel like minefields. You're rehearsing what to say before your own standups. Your strongest engineer has started going quiet and you know what that silence probably means.

So you've read 40% of a management book. You've asked your own manager, who was never trained either and said something like just be yourself. You've typed something into your phone at 1am that you'd rather not admit to.

Here's the thing: none of that is evidence you're failing.

It's evidence you're doing a job nobody explained — and you're trying to do it alone, at speed, while still writing code because at least code does what you tell it to.

The problem underneath all of it isn't delegation or feedback frameworks or any of the surface things.

It's that you don't yet know whether the 2am certainty you've been found out is a real signal or just the deep end.

Tomorrow I'll tell you what I think it is.

P.S. The strongest engineers I've worked with all started here. Every single one.

welcome_seq.preview: Most support for engineering managers smells wrong. There's a reason — and a reason this doesn't.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

You already know what bad support for engineering managers looks like.

It's the laminated framework. The workshop that covers communication techniques you could have googled. The coach who came up through HR or L&D and talks about competency development in a way that makes you want to close the laptop.

Engineers detect the difference inside ten minutes. It's not snobbery — it's pattern matching. You can tell whether someone has actually been the one who shipped late, had the redundancy conversation, stood in the stairwell afterwards and held it together long enough to get back to the team.

I was an engineering manager for nine years. I've done all of those things. I still remember what the deep end feels like from the inside, not from a case study.

That's what Deep End Coaching is built from.

Not a slide deck. Not a framework someone learned in a training room. The actual job, explained by someone who has done it — including the parts that don't go in the LinkedIn posts.

Most coaches came up through HR or L&D. The work I do came up through standups and skip-level meetings and difficult conversations I had to run before I felt ready.

Your job isn't to be the best engineer in the room anymore. It's to make the room better.

Someone told me that once. I'll tell you more about where it came from tomorrow.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply and tell me what kind of support you've already tried — I'm curious what's landed and what hasn't.

subject_variants.subject: How to run a difficult conversation without feeling sick
One thing to do before your next hard 1:1
The thing that changes how your team sees you

welcome_seq.preview: Something practical you can use before the end of the week.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Practical one today.

The biggest thing engineers get wrong in difficult conversations is walking in with a verdict already written.

You've rehearsed the thing you're going to say. You've decided what the situation means. You go in to deliver the message — and the person on the other side can feel that before you've finished your first sentence. The conversation closes down.

Here's what to do instead.

Walk in with one question you genuinely can't answer. Not a question you already know the answer to. Not a leading question designed to bring them around to your view. An actual gap: something about their situation, their experience of the team, what's making the work hard for them right now.

Ask it. Then stop talking.

This feels counterintuitive because you've been the person who solves problems by thinking harder. A difficult conversation is not that kind of problem. It's an information problem. You don't have enough of it yet.

The engineers who stop drowning in 1:1s are the ones who realise their job is to make the room better — and that starts with understanding what's actually in the room.

Slow down. Ask the question. Let the silence do some of the work.

You'll be better at that conversation than you think.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply and tell me what difficult conversation is on your calendar this week — I'll send you a follow-up thought.

This smells like motivational-poster content dressed up as something serious. That test exists for a reason. Nine years inside the actual engineering manager role — not an HR or L&D background — is why the work feels different. You'll know within ten minutes. I'd rather you know sooner.

You're already underwater and can't add six more hours. Six sessions over three months. One hour every two weeks. The engineers I work with almost always say it's the one hour that makes the other hours work better — including the standups and the 1:1s that are currently costing you energy they shouldn't.

What if it's just another laminated framework? It isn't. But I can't prove that in an email. The Lifeboat session exists so you can find out without committing the full amount first.

Tomorrow I'll tell you exactly what the next step looks like.

subject_variants.subject: What staying stuck in the deep end actually costs
The engineer who waits for it to click on its own
The longer the panic goes on, the more it takes

promo_seq.preview: Waiting is a decision. Here's what it's costing and what changes instead.
promo_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Most engineers who find their way to Deep End Coaching have been waiting.

Waiting for it to click on its own. Waiting until they feel more established. Waiting until they're sure they need it — as if needing it isn't already clear from the fact that they're rehearsing their own standups in the shower.

Here's what waiting looks like from the outside:

The strongest engineer on the team goes quiet. Then quieter. Then gone. The skip-level meeting where they say nothing useful cements a version of them in senior leadership's mind that takes months to undo. The 1:1s stay minefields because nobody has ever shown them a different approach — not a framework, an approach.

None of this is inevitable. But it compounds.

The engineers who stop drowning are the ones who decide that learning the job out loud, in front of someone, is allowed. That the 2am panic isn't evidence they were the wrong choice. That they don't have to perform a confidence they don't yet have until the performance collapses.

The Lifeboat session is 90 minutes and £250. It's built for the specific fire you have right now, and it tells you within that session whether the deeper work fits.

If you've been waiting — this is what you've been waiting for permission to do.

{{link}}
